discovery: Optical lattice atomic clocks reaching 10^-18 accuracy

nominees.name: Hidetoshi Katori
nominees.affiliation: University of Tokyo and RIKEN, Japan

nominees.name: Jun Ye
nominees.affiliation: JILA, NIST and University of Colorado Boulder, USA

subfield: Atomic, molecular and optical physics / precision measurement
motivation: Katori proposed and first demonstrated the optical lattice clock (2001-2005). In this clock, neutral atoms are trapped at a 'magic' wavelength, so the clock transition is not perturbed while thousands of atoms are interrogated together. Ye turned the concept into the world's most stable and accurate clocks. He combined ultrastable lasers, frequency combs and control of quantum many-body interactions to reach systematic uncertainties near 10^-18 and below. Katori showed that portable lattice clocks can measure gravitational redshift over height differences of centimetres, as in the Tokyo Skytree experiment. Ye resolved the redshift within a single millimetre-scale atomic sample. Together their work founded a new measurement paradigm: frequency standards two orders of magnitude beyond caesium, which have prompted the redefinition of the SI second. These clocks also enable relativistic geodesy and searches for dark matter and for variation of fundamental constants. This advance in precision measurement has reshaped fundamental physics.
